commits.pr_title: [Frontend][Mistral] Forward response_format to mistral-common chat templating
commits.pr_body:
## Overview Forward the OpenAI `response_format` to mistral-common so v15 tokenizers that declare a `json_schema` model setting render it into `[MODEL_SETTINGS]`. The Mistral tokenizer now forwards extra chat-template kwargs instead of special-casing `reasoning_effort` behind a version check. Related: #63797 opens the same feature. This PR is a smaller implementation of it: no conversion helper and no version guard (see Details). ## Claims - `json_object` and `json_schema` (with a schema) requests on Mistral models render the schema into `[MODEL_SETTINGS]`. Other formats are dropped, as before. - `MistralTokenizer.apply_chat_template` forwards its remaining kwargs (`reasoning_effort`, `response_format`, ...) to `MistralCommonBackend`, which forwards them to `ChatCompletionRequest.from_openai`. That function ignores fields it does not know, so tokenizers without these settings render exactly as before. - `/tokenize` accepts `response_format` for chat requests, so the rendered prompt can be inspected. ## Validation Rendered with an internal v15 tokenizer whose `model_settings_builder` declares `json_schema`, through `ChatCompletionRequest.build_chat_params` → `MistralRenderer` → `MistralTokenizer`, with `reasoning_effort="high"`: | `response_format` | `[MODEL_SETTINGS]` | | --- | --- | | `json_schema` (strict or not) | `{"json_schema": , "reasoning_effort": "high"}` | | `json_object` | `{"json_schema": {"anyOf": [{"type": "object"}, {"type": "array"}]}, "reasoning_effort": "high"}` | | `text`, `structural_tag`, none | `{"reasoning_effort": "high"}` | With `mistralai/Mistral-Small-4-119B-2603`, whose tokenizer has no `json_schema` setting, the prompt is unchanged for every format. ``` pytest tests/tokenizers_/test_mistral.py tests/renderers/test_mistral.py # 66 passed, 2 skipped ``` `tests/entrypoints/serve/tokenize/test_serving_tokenization.py` was not run locally (`orjson` is missing from my environment); it runs in CI. ## Details - No conversion helper: the OpenAI `response_format` dump (`by_alias=True`) already matches mistral-common's `ResponseFormat`, because `JsonSchema.custom_schema` has the alias `schema`. The renderer only drops formats mistral-common rejects: `structural_tag`, and `json_schema` without a schema. - No version guard: removing the `self.version >= 15` filter lets mistral-common decide what each tokenizer supports. The tokenizer keeps its explicit transformers arguments and pops them out of `kwargs`, so they are not passed twice. - Tests replace the pre-v15 omission test with a forwarding test, and add a test that calls the real tokenizer with the renderer's kwargs. ---

commits.pr_title: [CI][AMD] Mirror ReplaySSM, MiniMax-M3 attention kernels and Kimi K3 prefix cache on MI355
commits.pr_body:
Adds AMD mirrors for the three test groups in `test_areas` that still had none: ReplaySSM E2E, MiniMax-M3 Attention Kernels and Kimi K3 Prefix Cache. The Kimi K3 Prefix Cache mirror needs two fixes that have not landed yet (see Details).

- `engine.yaml`: ReplaySSM E2E on `mi355_2`. The FlashInfer-only cases in `test_replayssm_decode.py` skip off CUDA.
- `kernels.yaml`: MiniMax-M3 Attention Kernels on `mi355_dpx`, plus a test that checks the AITER indexer against a reference implementation.
- `models_basic.yaml`: Kimi K3 Prefix Cache on `mi355_4` with `VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER=1`. The existing MI355 Kimi K3 jobs now skip `test_prefix_cache.py` so it does not run twice.
- `test_prefix_cache.py`: on ROCm it gates on native MX support instead of SM100. The FlashInfer DCP xfail applies on CUDA only. The Mooncake transport can be set with `MOONCAKE_PROTOCOL` (default `rdma`), and the AMD mirror uses `tcp`.

## Validation

MI355 (gfx950), on current main with its ROCm pins (AITER `v0.1.25`, NIXL `1683cf3b`):

| Group | Runs | Result |
|---|---|---|
| ReplaySSM E2E | 10 | 10/10 pass (4 passed, 6 skipped each) |
| MiniMax-M3 Attention Kernels | 10 | 10/10 pass (161 passed, 14 skipped each) |
| Kimi K3 (existing job, with the new `--ignore`) | 1 | 336 passed, 67 skipped |
| Kimi K3 Prefix Cache, current main | 1 | 29 passed, 2 failed (`pd-tp2-dep2-block`/`-partial`, fixed by #61002) |
| Kimi K3 Prefix Cache, with #61002 and the AITER fix | 6 | 31/31 in 4 runs; the other 2 failed when another process on the shared node took the GPU memory |

## Details

The Kimi K3 Prefix Cache mirror depends on two fixes:

- #61002 (NixlConnector): pairs non-divisible hybrid MLA block sizes. Without it the two `pd-tp2-dep2` cases fail at the NIXL handshake.
- ROCm/aiter#6446: fixes an LL128 all-reduce deadlock that can hang the DCP cases under host contention. vLLM picks it up through an AITER release that includes it and a pin bump in `Dockerfile.rocm_base`. `v0.1.25` does not include it yet.

The new Mooncake test needs RDMA NICs (`mlx5_*`) by default, which MI355 runners may not have. The mirror runs it over TCP, which passes locally. The mirror inherits `optional` from the NVIDIA step, so like the 4xB200 job it runs nightly.

AI assistance (Claude Code) was used to draft this change. Every line was reviewed by the submitter.

---

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix][CUDA Graph] Weak-ref nested outputs of captured graphs
commits.pr_body:
<!-- markdownlint-disable -->

## Overview

`weak_ref_tensors` only weak-refs one level. For a model output like `(hidden_states, [aux_hidden_states, ...])`, the inner list is returned as is, so every captured CUDA graph entry keeps its aux hidden states alive and the graph pool cannot reuse that memory for the next capture size. This PR makes `weak_ref_tensors` recurse into nested lists/tuples.

Related: #63406 lists this as "aux hidden states kept by every PIECEWISE size" in its memory breakdown. This PR is the standalone fix and also applies to main's capture sizes.

## Claims

- Captured graphs no longer pin the aux hidden states used by EAGLE3, DSpark, DFlash and `extract_hidden_states`. Before, each captured size leaked `num_aux × num_tokens × hidden_size × dtype_size` bytes (3 × 8192 × 4096 × 2 B = 192 MiB for one 8192-token size of DeepSeek-V4-Flash).
- No output change: the outputs alias the same memory as before; only the references held by the graph entries become weak.
- `weak_ref_tensors` now raises on unknown types at any nesting level, not only at the top level, and passes ints and `LayerName`s through (piecewise subgraph outputs can contain ints, and Inductor graph partition outputs can contain `LayerName`s, see below).

## Validation

**Unit test** (`tests/utils_/test_torch_utils.py`, run by the "Async Engine, Inputs, Utils, Worker" CI step), on GB200:

```
# with this PR
pytest tests/utils_/test_torch_utils.py -v
39 passed

# torch_utils.py reverted to main, new tests only
pytest tests/utils_/test_torch_utils.py -v -k weak_ref
FAILED test_weak_ref_tensors_does_not_keep_nested_tensors_alive
E       AssertionError: assert 4194304 == (8388608 - 8388608)
FAILED test_weak_ref_tensors_rejects_unknown_nested_types
E       Failed: DID NOT RAISE ValueError
```

**What actually reaches `weak_ref_tensors`.** I wrapped the function in `vllm/compilation/cuda_graph.py` and `vllm/compilation/breakable_cudagraph.py`, then started each engine and recorded the structure of every input during capture (`T` = tensor; `[n:...]` = list of length n; `(n:...)` = tuple of length n):

| Model | CUDA graph path | Inputs seen |
|---|---|---|
| Qwen3-1.7B + EAGLE3 | torch.compile piecewise | `[1:T]` `[2:T]` `[4:T]` `[5:T]` `[6:T]` |
| Qwen3-1.7B + EAGLE3 | breakable | target `(2:T,[3:T])`, drafter `(2:T)` |
| gpt-oss-20b + EAGLE3 | torch.compile piecewise | `[1:T]` `[2:T]` `[5:T]` `[6:T]` |
| gpt-oss-20b + EAGLE3 | breakable | target `(2:T,[3:T])`, drafter `(2:T)` |
| Qwen3-30B-A3B-FP8 | torch.compile piecewise | `[1:T]` `[5:T]` `[6:T,int]` |
| Qwen3-30B-A3B-FP8 | breakable | `T` |

The nested case is the breakable target output with aux hidden states. The int case is a piecewise subgraph output of the FP8 MoE model, which is why ints are passed through. No `None`, float or 0-size tensor showed up.

The table does not cover `use_inductor_graph_partition=True`. There, on torch >= 2.11, `CUDAGraphWrapper` wraps each Inductor partition, and a partition's outputs can include `LayerName` objects that torch.compile hoists as graph inputs. This PR's first CI run caught it (`ValueError: Invalid type for tensors: <class 'vllm.utils.torch_utils.LayerName'>` in `test_full_cudagraph.py[*-partition=True]` and `test_full_graph.py::test_custom_compile_config`), so `LayerName`s pass through as well. After the fix, on GB200:

```
pytest compile/fullgraph/test_full_cudagraph.py -k "True and not MLA"
30 passed, 20 skipped (FA3, RocmAttn)

pytest compile/fullgraph/test_full_graph.py -k "compilation_config4 or compilation_config5"
2 passed
```

**End-to-end A/B**: DeepSeek-V4-Flash-DSpark, TP4+EP, DSpark K=7, 4×GB200. Breakable CUDA graph is on by default for this model, and capture sizes are main's defaults. Main is this PR's parent (2c58be22b6). Memory numbers are from TP rank 0.

| | main | this PR | Δ |
|---|---|---|---|
| CUDA graph pool, actual | 5.86 GiB | 5.39 GiB | −0.47 GiB |
| CUDA graph pool, profiler estimate | 8.55 GiB | 7.90 GiB | −0.65 GiB |
| Available KV cache memory | 112.94 GiB | 113.59 GiB | +0.65 GiB |
| GPU KV cache size | 7,277,119 tokens | 7,319,402 tokens | +0.58% |
| GSM8K 5-shot, flexible-extract | 0.9560 | 0.9522 | −5 / 1319 questions |
| DSpark acceptance (accepted / drafted) | 57.74% | 57.84% | |
| Mean acceptance length | 5.04 | 5.05 | |

The leak on main is about 0.65 GiB here, and it grows with the number and size of PIECEWISE capture sizes (#63406 raises both).

The 5-question GSM8K gap is from a single run per arm; serving is not batch invariant, so some run-to-run variance is expected. It does not indicate corrupted aux hidden states: they only feed the drafter, so corruption would lower acceptance, and acceptance is unchanged. The target model alone decides the output tokens under greedy rejection sampling.

<details>
<summary>Serve command</summary>

```bash
vllm serve deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-DSpark \
  --tensor-parallel-size 4 --enable-expert-parallel \
  --trust-remote-code --kv-cache-dtype fp8 --block-size 256 \
  --tokenizer-mode deepseek_v4 --reasoning-parser deepseek_v4 \
  --speculative-config '{"method":"dspark","num_speculative_tokens":7,"draft_sample_method":"greedy"}'
```

GSM8K: 5-shot, temperature 0, chat completions, thinking off. Acceptance is read from `vllm:spec_decode_*` metrics after the GSM8K run. Memory numbers come from the `CUDA graph pool memory`, `Available KV cache memory` and `GPU KV cache size` log lines.
</details>

## Details

**Affected paths.** `weak_ref_tensors` is called on capture outputs by:
- `BreakableCUDAGraphWrapper._capture`: captures the whole model forward, so EAGLE3/DSpark targets return `(hidden_states, [aux, ...])`. Breakable CUDA graph is on by default for DeepSeek-V4/V4.1, MiniMax-M3, GLM-5-Next, Kimi-K3 and others, under both model runners.
- `CUDAGraphWrapper` in FULL mode on MRV1, which also wraps the whole model.

Not affected: torch.compile piecewise subgraph outputs are flat, and MRV2 FULL graphs copy outputs into persistent buffers instead of weak-refing them.

**Safety of the weak refs.** Once the aux tensors are weak, later captures may reuse their memory, the same as for `hidden_states` today. So the aux tensors must be consumed before the next graph replay. Every consumer copies them first: MRV1 `torch.cat`/`torch.stack` in `gpu_model_runner.py`, MRV2 DFlash `_store_hidden_states` (concatenates into its staging buffer), MRV2 `extract_hidden_states` (`torch.stack` + `copy_`).

**Type contract.** Previously, non-tensor values inside a list/tuple passed through `weak_ref_tensor` silently, which is how the nested list slipped through. Now containers recurse, ints and `LayerName`s pass, and any other type raises with its type name. The tradeoff: a model whose capture output contains a leaf type not in the table above (e.g. `None`) fails at capture time instead of passing silently. The raise already caught one such case before (`IntermediateTensors`, #24275), and caught `LayerName` in this PR's first CI run.

**Not a duplicate:** no open PR touches `weak_ref_tensors` or this leak. #63406 changes capture sizes and only references the leak in its memory accounting.

The fix and analysis originate from Bo Pang (co-author). AI assistance (Claude Code) was used to write the change, the tests and the validation scripts.

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix][ROCm] Wait on per-slot events in packed NCCL consumer
commits.pr_body:
## Overview On ROCm, the packed NCCL consumer's per-slot `streams[i].synchronize()` can also wait for another slot's later `post_unpack_func` work, such as a layerwise reload replay. That stalls the host and removes the multi-buffer overlap. This PR waits on a per-slot event instead. Follow-up to #62555. ## Claims - Fixes the MI300X failure of `tests/distributed/test_packed_tensor.py::TestPackedBroadcastDeferredConsumer::test_freed_pack_not_reused_while_replay_pending` (all three parameterizations) when slot streams share a HIP hardware queue. The failure was seen in AMD CI. - Restores the overlap on ROCm when queues are shared. The consumer-only layerwise benchmark gets up to 7.9% faster on MI300X. - No regression on H100: every latency change is within ±0.41%, and memory is identical. ## Validation **Reproducer.** This uses the existing test. The bug only shows up when slot streams share a hardware queue. On the MI300X I tested (ROCm 7.14, torch 2.11) that doesn't happen at the default `GPU_MAX_HW_QUEUES=4`, so the test forces one queue: ```bash GPU_MAX_HW_QUEUES=1 pytest tests/distributed/test_packed_tensor.py -k replay_pending ``` | MI300X, `main` @ 533906528c | `GPU_MAX_HW_QUEUES` | `-k replay_pending` (3 cases) | full file (33 tests) | |---|---|---|---| | without this PR | 1 | **3/3 runs fail**: "the replay finished before every receive in the window was issued" | – | | with this PR | 1 | 3/3 runs pass | 33 passed | | without this PR | default (4) | pass | 33 passed | | with this PR | default (4) | pass | 33 passed | On H100 the full file passes with and without the change (33/33). **Performance.** Every run uses a fresh process. A and B alternate run by run, with 5 rounds of 20 timed calls each (3 rounds for end to end). Δ is the change in B's median versus A's. Noise is the larger standard deviation of the per-round medians. A result is significant if |Δ| > 2 × noise. - **Microbenchmarks:** - Consumer-only: one GPU with a fake broadcast. The payload is Llama-3-8B-shaped bf16 layers (4 or 16 GiB). `num_buffers` ∈ {2, 3}, packs of 64/256/1024 MiB. - Real RCCL/NCCL: producer on GPU 0, consumer on GPU 1. - Both run with `post_unpack_func` either copying immediately or replaying every 6 packs on the slot stream (layerwise). - **End to end:** the `examples/rl/rlhf_http_nccl.py` flow. Time is per weight update. OLMoE runs with real weights and `/weight_checker` checksums after every sync. | Benchmark | H100 (NVLink) | MI300X, queues = 1 | MI300X, default (4) / 16 queues | |---|---|---|---| | consumer-only, layerwise, 64 MiB packs | within ±0.41% | **−5.2% to −7.9%** (noise ≤ 1.3%) | +0.96 to +1.28% / +0.78 to +1.15% | | consumer-only, layerwise, 256 MiB packs | within ±0.41% | −1.2% to −1.5% | −0.69 to +1.38% / −0.05 to +1.06% | | consumer-only, all 24 configs | max +0.41% | – (layerwise only) | max +2.54% (noise 1.47%) / max +1.63% | | real RCCL/NCCL, all configs | within ±0.18% | within ±0.29% | within ±0.28% / ±0.37% | | E2E OLMoE-1B-7B, 128 MB packs (104 packs) | −3.2% (noise 0.6%) | – | −1.1% (noise 0.5%) | | E2E Qwen3-0.6B, 32 MB packs (36 packs) | −3.0% (noise 3.8%) | – | +1.8% (noise 2.0%) | | E2E opt-125m, 1 pack | +0.3% (noise 5.4%) | – | −0.2% (noise 0.5%) | At one queue, host time blocked in slot waits on MI300X goes from 11.5 ms to 8.9 ms per call (layerwise, 3 buffers, 64 MiB packs, 16 GiB). The final drain is unchanged. The real RCCL/NCCL path barely moves on MI300X: at about 49 GB/s the transfer dominates, so the stall is hidden. **Correctness:** every verify pass matched bit for bit: - 96 runs each on H100 and on MI300X at default queues; 24 per benchmark at one queue. - The weight checker found 0 mismatched syncs on A or B. - Generated outputs are identical with and without the change. **Memory:** peak allocated memory is identical in every config on both GPUs. Peak reserved memory is identical on H100, apart from one-pack allocator noise. On MI300X with one queue it is up to 3.1 GB higher with this PR in the layerwise configs. Receives now overlap the replay again, so PyTorch's caching allocator holds more blocks at once. Those figures stay at or below what both variants reserve at default queues.
Setup - **H100:** 4x H100 80GB (NV18), CUDA 13.0, torch 2.14.0+cu130, NCCL 2.30.7. Benchmarks ran on `e2b6723123` with and without this commit. End to end: TP=2 engine on GPUs 0–1, trainer on GPU 2. - **MI300X:** 2x MI300X (xGMI), ROCm 7.14, torch 2.11.0+rocm7.14.0, RCCL 2.30.4, in `rocm/vllm:rocm7.14.0_cdna_ubuntu24.04_py3.14_pytorch_2.11.0_vllm_0.23.0`, building this branch from source. End to end: TP=1 engine on GPU 1, trainer on GPU 0. RCCL rejects a trainer sharing a GPU with a TP rank, and only 2 GPUs were available. - **Rebase:** the reproducer table was rerun on current `main` (533906528c) after rebasing. The only change to this file since `e2b6723123` is #63457 (`torch.cuda` → `torch.accelerator` renames).
## Details **Root cause.** HIP multiplexes streams onto a small pool of hardware queues per process (`GPU_MAX_HW_QUEUES`, default 4). - **Before:** when two slot streams share a queue, `hipStreamSynchronize` on one also waits for work queued later on the other. The consumer's `streams[buffer_idx].synchronize()` before reusing slot `i` then waits for slot `j`'s `post_unpack_func` work, such as a layerwise replay. The host can't issue the next receive until that replay ends. The overlap the `num_buffers` window exists for is lost, and the test's assertion that the replay is still pending while the window's receives are issued fails. - **Why only ROCm:** CUDA streams don't serialize host synchronization this way. **Fix.** After `post_unpack_func`, record a `torch.Event` on the slot stream (`slot_done[buffer_idx]`). Before reusing the slot, wait on that event instead of synchronizing the stream. - **Same coverage:** the event covers the same work as before, the receive, unpack and `post_unpack_func` work on that slot's stream, but nothing queued after it. - **First use:** on a slot's first use there is nothing to wait for, so the wait is skipped. That's `num_buffers` fewer waits per call. - **Drain:** the closing `for stream in streams: stream.synchronize()` drain is unchanged. **Tradeoff.** The change adds one event record per pack. In the consumer-only microbenchmark with no queue sharing, B is about 0.4–1.6% slower on MI300X (beyond noise in some configs, with sub-millisecond packs), and within noise on H100. This doesn't show up with a real RCCL/NCCL transfer or end to end. **CI.** `tests/distributed/test_packed_tensor.py` already runs on AMD CI, which is where the failure appeared. No new test is added. Whether the existing test catches a regression of this fix depends on the runner's queue assignment. Forcing `GPU_MAX_HW_QUEUES=1` reproduces it every time. ---

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix][Core] Copy every overlaid KV view in copy_kv_cache_blocks_inplace
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

`copy_kv_cache_blocks_inplace` (the CoW copy for partial prefix-cache hits) skips a KV cache view when another view with the same `data_ptr` has already been copied. That is right for cross-layer KV sharing (identical aliased views) but wrong for hybrid models: the KV cache config puts one layer of each KV cache group on the same tensor, so a Mamba state view and an attention view share a base address while spanning different bytes per block, and whichever view comes first in layer order decides how many bytes of a block get copied.

For Kimi-K3 (3 KDA groups + 1 MLA group, block_size 5760, kernel page 64) the KDA view `(num_blocks, 1, 1, 814080)` int8 comes first, so the MLA view `(num_blocks*90, 1, 64, 576)` bf16 of the same tensor is skipped and an MLA block copy moves only 814080 of its 6635520 bytes, i.e. the first 706 of 5760 token slots. The whole-storage fast path would hide this, but it is not taken when several tensors live in one allocation.

Observed effect (het-TP PD, TP8 prefill -> TP1 decode, `--prefix-match-unit 128`, GSM8K 5-shot): every prompt's prefill stops at its last 128-token boundary `B` (Mamba align mode caches the state there); on the small-KV prefill engine the request is then preempted and resumes with a local partial prefix-cache hit on its own boundary entry, which redirects every group's block through this CoW copy (any new request with a partial hit takes the same path). The block the request continues in and ships to decode reads `slots [0,707) valid | [707,B) zero | [B,N-1) valid`. Accuracy dropped to 0.72 with a 128-token sawtooth (about 0.2 right after a boundary, 0.95 late in a chunk), only for `B >= 768`, deterministic per prompt and independent of the KDA kernel. Decode-local prefill on TP1 was unaffected because its per-block Mamba state is 8x larger (5653 slots), which is why the problem only showed up with a high-TP prefill engine.

## Fix

Key the dedup on `(device, data_ptr, shape, stride, element_size)`, so only identical aliased views are skipped and every overlaid geometry is copied. Overlaid views copy the same source block, so the extra narrow copy is redundant but harmless.

### Why the deduplication key includes view geometry

The key answers: "Has this view's block copy already been performed?" The same starting address does not imply the same copy coverage.

Consider the layout used by the regression test: four scheduler blocks per tensor region, 64 bytes per block, and two 256-byte tensor regions in one 512-byte storage. Within each region, a narrow Mamba view and a wider attention view start at the same address:

```text
One scheduler block:
byte offset     0              24                         64
                |--------------|--------------------------|
Mamba view      |  state data  |
Attention view  |              full KV data               |
```

The two views have these properties:

| Property | Mamba view | Attention view |
|---|---|---|
| Device | CPU | CPU |
| Starting address | A | A |
| Shape | (4, 1, 1, 24) | (8, 1, 8, 2) |
| Stride, in elements | (64, 1, 1, 1) | (16, 16, 2, 1) |
| Element size | 1 byte (int8) | 2 bytes (int16) |
| Bytes covered per scheduler block | 24 | 64 |

The attention view splits each scheduler block into two kernel pages: each page contains `1 * 8 * 2 = 16` int16 elements, so the two pages cover `2 * 16 * 2 = 64` bytes.

When copying block 0 to block 2, with the Mamba view visited first:

1. **Before the fix:** both views have the key `(device, A)`. The Mamba view copies the first 24 bytes and records the key. The attention view is then skipped, leaving the remaining 40 destination bytes unchanged.
2. **After the fix:** the views have different geometry keys. The Mamba view copies the first 24 bytes, and the attention view subsequently copies all 64 bytes. The overlapping 24 bytes are copied from the same source block to the same destination block, so the extra copy is redundant but harmless.

This example deliberately uses two tensor regions in one storage. The whole-storage fast path requires `storage.nbytes() == num_blocks * scheduler_block_stride`; here that is `512 == 4 * 64`, which is false. The fallback copies the current view's logical elements, so the narrow view cannot cover the full attention block. With a single 256-byte region, the whole-storage fast path would copy the full block and hide the bug.

The new key describes both the starting location and the layout:

```python
key = (
    cache.device,
    cache.data_ptr(),
    tuple(cache.shape),
    tuple(cache.stride()),
    cache.element_size(),
)
```

- `device` and `data_ptr()` identify where the view starts.
- `shape` describes its logical extent.
- `stride()` describes where its elements lie. For example, two views starting at `a` with shape `(3,)` can select `[a, b, c]` with stride 1 or `[a, c, e]` with stride 2.
- `element_size()` converts element-based strides to byte distances: stride 2 means 2 bytes for int8 but 4 bytes for int16.

Matching these fields lets identical aliased views retain the existing deduplication optimization without skipping overlaid views that cover different bytes.

## Test Plan

- New `tests/v1/worker/test_attn_utils.py::test_copy_kv_cache_blocks_overlaid_views_copy_whole_block`: two tensors in one storage, each with a narrow Mamba view listed before a wide attention view at the same address. Fails before the fix (only the first 24 of 64 bytes of the block are copied), passes after.
- `pytest tests/v1/worker/test_attn_utils.py`: 16 passed.
- E2E: Kimi-K3 het-TP PD (TP8 prefill, TP1/DP16 decode, NIXL + Mooncake Store), GSM8K 5-shot, 1319 prompts:

  | | before fix | with fix |
  |---|---|---|
  | exact_match (strict) | 0.7218 / 0.7286 (two runs) | **0.9682** |
  | decode-side MLA page scans with interior all-zero pages | 344 of 347 requests with B >= 768 | 0 of 31656 scans |

  (Second pass of the same run pending; decode-only baseline for this model is ~0.964.)

## Notes

- No open PR touches `copy_kv_cache_blocks_inplace` (searched `copy_kv_cache_blocks_inplace`, `kv_cache_block_copies`, `CoW block copy hybrid`).
- AI-assisted (Claude Code); the analysis, fix and test were reviewed line by line and the tests above were run by the submitter.

## Overview

Add the missing opt-in MiniMax-M3 MI355X MXFP4 AgentX preset from [InferenceX #4418](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX/pull/4418). Replace the stale #2959 guide-only reproduction with the current pinned-image profile, without changing general serving defaults or existing presets.

## Claims

- Twelve points: TP4 at c1/4/5/8/10/12/15/20/24/32 enables `--monokernel`; TP2 c1/c2 omits it. Each has `max-num-seqs = 2 × concurrency`, Model Runner V2, and no offload or expert parallelism.

The pinned monokernel handles supported physical decode widths 1–16; larger/mixed steps use ordinary decode. This documents the measured profile and makes no general performance/accuracy guarantee.

## Validation

Frozen source: [`f10885621773d1f900b6b4d002ee37863e583af3`](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX/tree/f10885621773d1f900b6b4d002ee37863e583af3), [`agg-variants.yaml`](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX/blob/f10885621773d1f900b6b4d002ee37863e583af3/inferencex-e2e/benchmarks/single_node/srt-slurm-recipes/minimaxm3/vllm/mi355x-fp4-mtp/agg-variants.yaml), key `minimaxm3-fp4-mi355x-vllm-agentic-mtp`.

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix] Fix Triton prefill attention OutOfResources on GPUs with 99KiB shared memory
commits.pr_body:
## Overview

Fixes #60847.

`google/embeddinggemma-2` crashes in engine warmup with Triton `OutOfResources` (`Required: 163840, Hardware limit: 101376`) on GPUs with 99 KiB of shared memory per block, such as RTX 30/40/50 cards and L4. The cause is that `context_attention_fwd` picks its tile size from the dtype and compute capability only. This change keeps halving the tile on CUDA until its Q, K and P tiles fit the device's opt-in shared memory per block.

Compared with #60848, this fix:

- Keeps every tile that already fits. [#60848](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/60847). estimates the need as `3*B*D`, which is up to 50% above what the kernel really needs. So on A100 it halves tiles that launch fine today, for example bf16 head size 256 (128 → 64) on this model's sliding layers. On an RTX 5090, halving a tile that fits made this kernel 1.18x to 1.65x slower.
- Adds a test that also catches the fp32 head-size-512 failure (`Required: 135168`). The test in [#60848](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/60847) adds only D=256, so it would also pass with a fix that leaves that path broken.

Compared with #60631, this fix:

- Also fixes the reported model in float32. With [#60631](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/60631), `vllm serve google/embeddinggemma-2 --runner pooling --dtype float32` still dies at engine start with `OutOfResources ... Required: 135168, Hardware limit: 101376`, from the same `context_attention_fwd` launch.
- Fits the tile for every head size, not only 256. With [#60631](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/60631), on 99 KiB GPUs, bf16 head sizes 192, 320, 384, 576 and 1024 still fail, and so do fp32 head sizes 320 to 512. bf16 head sizes 320 and 384 also still fail on A100 and H100.

## Claims

- `vllm serve google/embeddinggemma-2 --runner pooling` now starts and serves embeddings on a GPU with 99 KiB of shared memory, in bf16 (the command from the issue) and in fp32. Before the fix, engine warmup failed with `OutOfResources`.
- On such GPUs, `context_attention_fwd` now launches for every tested bf16/fp16 head size from 160 to 1024 and for fp32 head sizes 320, 384 and 512. All of these failed before.
- Tiles that already launched do not change. Output is bitwise the same for every configuration that worked before.
- `test_context_attention` gets D=256 and D=512. 8 of the new cases fail on the old code on a 99 KiB GPU and pass with the fix.

## Validation

Hardware: 1x NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090 (compute capability 12.0, driver 615.71.09). It has 101376 bytes of opt-in shared memory per block, the same limit as the RTX 5070 Ti and RTX 3060 in the issue. Software: vLLM `0.31.1rc1.dev173+g8cbd5d030` (commit `8cbd5d03006c`), and this change on top of it.

Reproducer. No request is needed, because the failure happens at startup:

```bash
VLLM_ENGINE_READY_TIMEOUT_S=3600 vllm serve google/embeddinggemma-2 --runner pooling --dtype bfloat16 \
  --limit-mm-per-prompt '{"image":0,"audio":0,"video":0}' --max-model-len 4096
```

Before: all 4 runs failed in engine warmup. 3 ran in the `vllm/vllm-openai:nightly-8cbd5d03006c33185f402249ff2b448efd594986` image (torch 2.13.0+cu130, triton 3.7.1). 1 ran from an editable install of the same commit.

```
File ".../vllm/v1/attention/backends/triton_attn.py", line 784, in _forward_encoder_attention
File ".../vllm/v1/attention/ops/triton_prefill_attention.py", line 270, in context_attention_fwd
triton.runtime.errors.OutOfResources: out of resource: shared memory, Required: 163840, Hardware limit: 101376. Reducing block sizes or `num_stages` may help.
RuntimeError: Engine core initialization failed. See root cause above. Failed core proc(s): {}
```

After: all 3 runs passed warmup with the same `TRITON_ATTN` backend and reached `Application startup complete`. `POST /v1/embeddings` returned 200 OK. The logs have no `Traceback` and no `OutOfResources`. The same command with `--dtype float32` also starts and serves.

Embedding values: I compared the served embeddings with `transformers` 5.19 in fp32 on CPU (mean pooling, then normalize). Cosine similarity was 0.99996 for the 9-token and 1492-token inputs and 0.99995 for a 4092-token input. The 4092-token input goes past the 512-token sliding window.

Kernel tests:

```bash
pytest tests/kernels/attention/test_triton_prefill_attention.py
```

- With the fix: 41 passed.
- Old kernel file with the new test file (`-k "test_context_attention and not sliding"`): 8 failed, 16 passed. The failures are bf16 D=256 (`Required: 163840`) and fp32 D=512 (`Required: 135168`).
- These tests ran with `--noconftest`, because the test venv did not have `tblib`.
- The new cases fail on the old code only on GPUs with less than 160 KiB per block, such as L4 or RTX cards. On H100 they pass with or without the fix.

Old and new kernel side by side: both ran on the same inputs (sequences of 37, 300 and 700 tokens, 8 query heads, 2 KV heads, non-causal), and each output was compared with fp32 SDPA:

| dtype | head size | before | after |
|---|---|---|---|
| fp16, bf16 | 32, 64, 80, 96, 128, 512 | OK | OK, bitwise the same |
| fp16, bf16 | 160, 192, 256, 320, 384, 576, 768, 1024 | `OutOfResources` | OK, error 0.0005 (fp16), 0.0036 to 0.0045 (bf16) |
| fp32 | 32 to 256 | OK | OK, bitwise the same |
| fp32 | 320, 384, 512 | `OutOfResources` | OK, error 0.0020 to 0.0025 |
| fp32 | 576, 768, 1024 | `OutOfResources` | `OutOfResources` |

`pre-commit run --files` on both changed files passed.

## Details

Root cause: `context_attention_fwd` sets `BLOCK_M = BLOCK_N = BLOCK` from `get_block_size(dtype)`. That returns 128 for bf16/fp16 on any GPU with capability 8.0 or higher, and 32 for fp32. The only other rule is `if Lk >= 512: BLOCK = min(BLOCK, 32)`. The kernel keeps a Q tile, a K tile and a P tile in shared memory. For bf16, head size 256 and BLOCK 128, that is `2 * (128*256 + 128*256 + 128*128) = 163840` bytes. A100 (166912) and H100/B200 (232448) have room for it, but sm_86, sm_89, sm_120 and sm_121 GPUs have only 101376. EmbeddingGemma2 has head size 256 on its sliding layers and 512 on its full layers, so vLLM forces `TRITON_ATTN`. Its bidirectional layers go through `_forward_encoder_attention` → `context_attention_fwd`. The 512 layers already get BLOCK 32 and fit. The 256 layers do not fit. The same problem breaks bf16/fp16 head size 192 and fp32 head size 512 (135168 bytes).

Fix: on CUDA, after the existing choices, halve BLOCK until `element_size * BLOCK * (2 * D + BLOCK)` fits in `get_max_shared_memory_bytes()` (`cudaDevAttrMaxSharedMemoryPerBlockOptin`). Here D is `next_power_of_2(Lk)`. BLOCK never goes below 16, the smallest tile `tl.dot` accepts. The result is cached per (block, head size, element size), so each call costs one cache lookup.

The formula comes from `_fwd_kernel.warmup().metadata.shared` on sm_120. For large head sizes it matches the real use exactly. For small head sizes it is higher than the real use. This holds for all 60 configurations measured. I do not claim it is an upper bound on every GPU: a review found that it under-counts fp16 use on sm_75, but the tiles it picks there still fit.

Effect on 99 KiB GPUs: head sizes up to 128 keep 128. bf16/fp16 head size 192 or 256 goes from 128 to 64 (73728 bytes). fp32 head size 512 goes from 32 to 16. On A100, bf16 head size 256 keeps 128 and fp32 head size 512 keeps 32.

Limitations:

- ROCm does not change (there is an `is_cuda()` gate). The formula was measured on NVIDIA's Triton backend. On MI300 (65536 bytes of LDS) it would shrink the common head-size-128 tile, and I could not check if that is needed. Head-size-256 encoder attention on 64 KiB ROCm GPUs may have the same bug. I did not test it.
- fp32 with head size above 512 still fails on 99 KiB GPUs, because 16 is the smallest tile. It also failed before this change.
- `get_max_shared_memory_bytes()` reads GPU 0 and keeps the first value it reads. On a host with mixed GPU types, the limit comes from one GPU. Other users of this helper have the same limit.
- The cache key does not include the limit, so a test that mocks a different limit in the same process can get a stale tile. The existing mocked tests `test_kv_tile_width_is_gated_by_platform` and `test_rdna_narrows_the_kv_tile_and_nothing_else` now read the real limit on CUDA. They pass on the RTX 5090. On a GPU with less than 98304 bytes, the `[not-rocm]` case would see tile 64.

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix][Spec Decode] Apply the draft max_model_len limit before model config hooks
commits.pr_body:
## Overview

Fixes #63844. On Model Runner V2, a hybrid Mamba/attention target with prefix caching disabled and a draft whose `max_model_len` is below the target's fails config validation with `--mamba-block-size can only be set with --enable-prefix-caching`, although the flag was never set. Regression from #63251.

## Claims

- `VllmConfig` now lowers `max_model_len` to the draft's before running the model `verify_and_update_config` hooks, so values they derive from it (here the default `mamba_block_size`) use the final length.
- The reported command starts on V2; V1 and non-hybrid models are unchanged.

## Validation

New test `test_draft_limit_applies_before_hybrid_mamba_block_size` goes through `EngineArgs.create_engine_config()`, the path shared by `LLM` and `vllm serve` (CPU, only config files are fetched).

Before (fix reverted):

```text
$ pytest tests/config/test_speculative_draft_limits_max_model_len.py -k hybrid
E       pydantic_core._pydantic_core.ValidationError: 1 validation error for VllmConfig
E         Value error, --mamba-block-size can only be set with --enable-prefix-caching
1 failed, 4 deselected
```

After:

```text
$ pytest tests/config/test_speculative_draft_limits_max_model_len.py tests/config/test_speculative_draft_max_position_embeddings.py
20 passed
```

Wider suite `pytest tests/config tests/test_config.py` (macOS, CPU-only, `test_ray_runtime_env` deselected since Ray isn't installed): 771 passed, 29 failed. All 29 fail identically on `main` without this change (gated `meta-llama` repos, model inspection failing for multimodal architectures on this platform, CPU-specific compilation defaults, and V1-runner async-scheduling checks), so none are introduced here.

End to end, the reproducer from #63844 (`--load-format dummy`, CPU) now passes config validation; before the fix it raised the error above from `create_engine_config`:

```bash
VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=1 vllm serve ai21labs/Jamba-tiny-random --max-model-len 4096 \
  --no-enable-prefix-caching --load-format dummy \
  --speculative-config '{"method":"draft_model","model":"ai21labs/Jamba-tiny-random","num_speculative_tokens":3,"max_model_len":1024}'
```

The test runs in the CPU "Multimodal + Config" Buildkite step (`pytest -v -s config`, depends on `vllm/config/`). `pre-commit run` passes on the changed files.

## Details

Root cause: #63251 added `_limit_max_model_len_to_draft()` after `try_verify_and_update_config()`. For hybrid models with prefix caching off, `MambaModelConfig.verify_and_update_config` sets `mamba_block_size = max_model_len` (4096). The limit then lowers `max_model_len` to 1024, and the after-validator `validate_mamba_block_size` reads `mamba_block_size != max_model_len` as a user-set flag.

Moving the limit ahead of the hooks is safe: it only reads the speculative config and `use_v2_model_runner`, which depends on `speculative_config`, `lora_config`, and `parallel_config` fields (executor backend, PP/DCP/PCP sizes, ubatching) that the hooks do not write. Hooks that also lower `max_model_len` (e.g. the 8192 cap for EmbeddingGemma2) still apply, now on top of the draft limit, so the result is the same minimum. Other values the hooks derive from `max_model_len`, such as `rotary_kwargs["max_position"]`, also see the final length now.

Not a duplicate: no open PR references #63844 or `_limit_max_model_len_to_draft`. #52045 works around the same validator for a different trigger (CPU MLA disabling prefix caching) and does not touch this ordering.

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix][ROCm][DSv4] Give zero and subnormal mono MXFP8 groups vLLM's scale code
commits.pr_body: - `stages/moe.py` (`vllm_mx_code`) and `attention/device.py` (`mx_code`) in the DeepSeek-V4 and V4.1 mono decode kernels: when `q = RN(max(amax, FLT_MIN) / 448)` is an f32 subnormal, return code 0 for `q <= 2^-127` and 1 above it, instead of the exponent-bit result, which is always 1 The four copies take the E8M0 scale code from the exponent bits of `q`. Their docstrings, and vLLM's `mxfp8_e4m3_quantize`, give `clamp(ceil(log2 q) + 127, 0, 254)`. For a subnormal `q` the bit trick gives 1, so every group with `amax <= 448 * 2^-127`, including all-zero groups, gets code 1 where vLLM gives 0. The monokernel I/O tests in #63486 catch this, and it blocks that PR. In practice, zero groups (for example a zeroed norm-weight group) only get a different scale byte and still dequantize to 0. bf16-valued inputs never dequantize differently. Only the f32 attention-output quant (XO) could, for groups with amax below 2.6e-36. | amax | q | before | after | vLLM rule (Triton / torch op) | |---|---|---|---|---| | 0 | FLT_MIN / 448 | 1 | 0 | 0 / 0 | | 1e-36 | subnormal | 1 | 0 | 0 / 0 | | 448 * 2^-127 | 2^-127 | 1 | 0 | 0 / 0 | | prev(448 * 2^-126) | rounds to 2^-126 | 1 | 1 | 1 / 1 | | 1.0 | normal | 119 | 119 | 119 / 119 | | check (MI355X) | before | after | |---|---|---| | every non-negative finite f32 amax (2,139,095,040), each of the 4 copies | 73,400,322 wrong codes | 0 | | `test_mono_primitives.py -k scale_codes` (#63486) | 4 failed | 5 passed | | DSv4.1 layer test, hard case with a zeroed norm group | 48 of 7680 codes wrong per quant, 16/16 runs | 0, 10/10 runs | | f32-valued tiny groups, dequantized vs vLLM | 195,270 elements differ | 0 | Decode step time, 20-step CUDA graph, median of interleaved runs (DSv4.1 TP4: 10 runs per arm; DSv4-Pro TP8: pooled runs), with #63576 applied in every DSv4.1 arm: | case | before (us) | after (us) | delta | |---|---|---|---| | DSv4.1 1x1, index source | 75.94 | 76.66 | +0.94% | | DSv4.1 1x6, index source | 102.86 | 103.03 | +0.17% | | DSv4.1 8x6, index source | 314.73 | 314.95 | +0.07% | | DSv4.1 8x6, hard case | 170.75 | 170.67 | -0.05% | | DSv4-Pro 1x1 | 90.69 | 90.79 | +0.11% | | DSv4-Pro 1x7 | 124.45 | 124.41 | -0.03% | | DSv4-Pro 64x1 | 412.24 | 412.84 | +0.15% | An unchanged-code control arm moved -0.21% to +0.11% on DSv4-Pro and +0.10 us on DSv4.1. The one case outside that is DSv4.1 at one row with an index source: +0.7 us in two 5-round sets and +0.3 us in a follow-up. The same step without the index source doesn't move, and K1's eager device time is unchanged (18.22 vs 18.05 us). AI assistance (Claude Code) was used to draft this change. commits.pr_title: [Bugfix][MRV2] Release the warmup memory cached on the capture streams
commits.pr_body:
## Overview

Empty the caching allocator once at the end of the Model Runner V2 `capture_model()`, before it reads free memory, so that warmup activations cached on the discarded capture streams are released. Fixes #63052.

## Claims

- With breakable CUDA graphs and no FULL graphs (`cudagraph_mode=PIECEWISE`), the largest warmup's activations stay reserved on the capture stream for the life of the process and are reported as CUDA graph memory. On DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash prefill (GB200, DP4) that is 10.49 GiB per rank; this PR releases it.
- Modes with FULL graphs already end in this state, because `torch.cuda.graph()` empties the cache before each FULL capture.
- 3 lines; graph pools and allocated memory are unchanged.

## Validation

GB200, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash prefill, DP4, `max_model_len` 1M, breakable graphs with capture sizes up to 16384 tokens, v0.32.0-based build. Per rank, at the end of `capture_model()`, with the default-pool segments of `torch.cuda.memory._snapshot()` grouped by stream:

| | `PIECEWISE` (`main`) | `PIECEWISE` + `empty_cache()` at the end | `FULL_AND_PIECEWISE` (`main`) |
|---|---|---|---|
| model capture stream: reserved (in use) | 7.93 (1.77) GiB | 2.43 (1.77) GiB | 2.43 (1.77) GiB |
| replay capture stream: reserved (in use) | 6.65 (1.65) GiB | 1.70 (1.65) GiB | 1.70 (1.65) GiB |
| graph capture memory (free-memory delta) | 26.39 GiB | 15.90 GiB | 21.00 GiB |
| `memory_allocated()` at the end | 119.12 GiB | 119.12 GiB | 119.16 GiB |

- The first two columns differ by 10.49 GiB per rank, all of it cached warmup memory. The graph pools (5.63 + 5.18 GiB), the allocated memory, and a smoke test are the same in both.
- The middle column comes from a diagnostic run that calls `empty_cache()` at the same point, after taking the snapshot above. This exact commit has not been run on a GPU.
- `FULL_AND_PIECEWISE` also captures 44 FULL decode graphs and 39 FULL DSpark graphs, so its total is higher; its capture streams end up in the same state as the middle column.

No test is added: the effect needs a breakable PIECEWISE capture whose warmup is large enough to matter, and CI has no runner for that configuration.

## Details

**Root cause.**

1. `capture_model()` empties the cache once before capturing, and reads free memory at the end without emptying it again.
2. Each `CudaGraphManager.capture()` enters `graph_capture()`, which creates a new stream, and runs every size eagerly once before capturing it. The caching allocator keeps the freed warmup blocks on that stream. Sizes are captured largest first, so the cache ends up holding the largest warmup's peak, and nothing allocates on that stream afterwards.
3. `capture_model()` runs under `freeze_gc_for_cudagraph_capture()`. While gc is frozen, breakable capture skips its per-descriptor `gc.collect()` + `empty_cache()` (#54646).
4. With FULL graphs, `torch.cuda.graph.__enter__` empties the cache before each FULL capture and releases these blocks as a side effect. With PIECEWISE only, nothing does.

The blocks are released only when some caching-allocator allocation fails and the allocator frees all cached blocks to retry. Allocations outside the caching allocator (NCCL, NVSHMEM, CUDA module loading) see the memory as used.

**KV budget.** `profile_cudagraph_memory()` measures `capture_model(profile_only=True)`, so the CUDA graph estimate subtracted from the KV budget also includes these blocks today; with this change it no longer does (from reading the code; the KV cache size was not measured). This complements #59368, which measures the graph pool for the estimate: with #59368 alone, the estimate would exclude this cache while the real capture still holds it.

**Tradeoff.** As noted in #50780, on a model whose profile run under-counts long-prefill activations, these cached blocks acted as reclaimable headroom. With this change that memory goes to the KV cache instead, which is the state `FULL_AND_PIECEWISE` already ends in.

Related: #62965 (the decoder replay graphs' separate stream and pool).

commits.pr_title: [Spec Decode][Sampling] Batch-sharded draft logits
commits.pr_body:
## Context
During batch-sharded sampling, the target logits are sharded along the token dimension. The requests are deterministically assigned to ranks using the formula: `req_state_idx % tp_size`. So during TP=4, rank 0 only samples (and in the case of spec decoding verifies) requests with state indices: 0, 4, 8, 12, ....

Currently, draft model-derived speculators allocate persistent draft logits tensors to hold all requests up to `max-num-seqs`, which is wasteful during batch-sharded sampling because only `max-num-seqs // TP` of those request logits are actually used by each rank. Sharding the draft logits can enable us to save GPU memory.

## This PR

Under batch-sharded sampling, each rank now allocates draft logits only for the requests it verifies. The draft logits cache shrinks from `max_num_seqs` rows to `cdiv(max_num_seqs, tp_size)` rows per rank, and the freed memory goes to the KV cache.

**Layout.** A request's draft logits live only on its owner rank, at row `req_state_idx // tp_size`. Two Triton helpers in `batch_shard.py` define the pair: `shard_owner` (`req_state_idx % num_shards`, the existing owner rule) and `shard_row` (`req_state_idx // num_shards`). Every write and read of the cache goes through them. With one shard both reduce to the current behavior and compile away.

**Writes.** Drafting stays replicated, so every rank still samples every draft token and no new collectives are added. Each rank writes only the rows it owns:
- `gumbel_sample` takes `logits_cache_num_shards` / `logits_cache_shard_idx` and masks its cache store to the owner rank. `DraftModelSpeculator.sample_draft` and DSpark's `_sample_logits` pass them through.
- DFlash2's `_cache_draft_logits_kernel`, which writes only the top-k candidate columns, applies the same mask.

**Reads.** `RejectionSampler` takes `draft_logits_num_shards`, and the rejection kernels index draft logits with `shard_row(req_state_idx, DRAFT_LOGITS_NUM_SHARDS)`.

**Allocation.** The cache moves from `DraftModelSpeculator.__init__` to `load_model`, so it is allocated once at its final size after the target and draft models are loaded. It is sharded when all of these hold:
- batch-sharded sampling is active for the target (`batch_sharded_sampling_enabled`, a new helper that the model runner also uses to create the `BatchSharder`),
- the speculator opts in via `supports_batch_sharded_draft_logits()`,
- no draft watermarker is configured.

The model runner passes `speculator.draft_logits_num_shards` to the `RejectionSampler`. It also asserts that a custom rejection sampler never receives a sharded cache.

**Speculators that opt in:** every one whose cache writes honor the owner mask.
- `TargetDependentARSpeculator`: Eagle, MTP, Gemma4.
- `StandaloneARSpeculator` and `MultiModuleMTPSpeculator`.
- `DFlashSpeculator`, and through it DSpark, XPress, DFlash2 and LiLiCorr.
- **Exception:** DSpark keeps the full cache when the draft model provides its own fused `sample_sequential` (the AMD DeepSeek-V4.1 path), because those kernels write the full-size cache.

**Memory freed per rank** (TP4, `max_num_seqs=256`, probabilistic drafts), from server startup logs:

| Target + draft | Draft logits cache, base → shard | KV cache memory, base → shard | KV cache tokens |
|---|---|---|---|
| DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash + DSpark (K=5) | 0.31 → 0.08 GiB | 74.44 → 74.67 GiB | +0.31% |
| Qwen3.6-27B + MTP (K=3) | 0.36 → 0.09 GiB | 150.69 → 150.96 GiB | +0.18% |
| Qwen3.6-27B + DFlash (K=7) | 0.83 → 0.21 GiB | 145.77 → 146.39 GiB | +0.43% |
| Qwen3.8-27B + DFlash2 (K=7, fp32 cache) | 1.66 → 0.41 GiB | 147.07 → 148.31 GiB | +0.85% |

## Benchmarks

No regression in accuracy or acceptance rate for any speculator that now writes batch-sharded draft logits.

**Setup:** 4x GB200, TP4, `draft_sample_method=probabilistic`, prefix caching off, natural EOS. Each pair ran 4 server boots in the order base, shard, shard, base. "base" is `--enable-batch-sharded-sampling` off and "shard" is on. Startup logs confirmed every shard boot sharded the draft logits cache on all 4 ranks.

- **GSM8K:** `tests/evals/gsm8k/gsm8k_eval.py`, 1319 questions. t0 is temperature 0, one run per boot. t1 is temperature 1 with 3 seeds per boot, 6 runs per arm. The Qwen models use chat completions with thinking disabled.
- **SPEED-Bench:** `low_entropy` subset, `throughput_2k` config, concurrency 64, 256 prompts, temperature 1, top_p 1.
- **Acceptance length** = 1 + accepted / drafts, from the server's Prometheus metrics.
- Each cell shows the mean over the arm's runs.

### GSM8K accuracy

| Target + draft | K | t0 base | t0 shard | t1 base | t1 shard |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash + DSpark | 5 | 0.907 | 0.906 | 0.816 | 0.807 |
| Qwen3.6-27B + MTP | 3 | 0.969 | 0.970 | 0.968 | 0.967 |
| Qwen3.6-27B + DFlash | 7 | 0.970 | 0.970 | 0.966 | 0.966 |
| Qwen3.8-27B + DFlash2 | 7 | 0.964 | 0.961 | 0.960 | 0.960 |

### Acceptance length

| Target + draft | GSM8K t0 base | GSM8K t0 shard | GSM8K t1 base | GSM8K t1 shard | SPEED-Bench base | SPEED-Bench shard |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash + DSpark | 3.554 | 3.540 | 3.275 | 3.283 | 3.546 | 3.556 |
| Qwen3.6-27B + MTP | 3.617 | 3.619 | 3.519 | 3.515 | 3.258 | 3.271 |
| Qwen3.6-27B + DFlash | 5.499 | 5.490 | 4.980 | 4.984 | 3.905 | 3.927 |
| Qwen3.8-27B + DFlash2 | 6.164 | 6.152 | 5.876 | 5.890 | 3.636 | 3.647 |

### SPEED-Bench noise check (Qwen3.6-27B + MTP)

Every pair read 0.3–0.6% higher acceptance on SPEED-Bench with sharding. To check whether that was real, I ran a third arm that shards verification but keeps the draft logits cache replicated. I ran each arm with top-k on and off, with 2 boots per arm.

| Arm | top_k=20 (model default) | top_k disabled |
|---|---|---|
| base | 3.266 | 3.268 |
| sharded verification, replicated draft logits | 3.263 | 3.262 |
| sharded verification, sharded draft logits | 3.263 | 3.261 |

The three arms match. Base alone ranged from 3.254 to 3.279 across boots, so the shift is boot-to-boot noise.

### Notes

- **DFlash2 GSM8K t0, 0.964 → 0.961:** a 4-question difference. At temperature 0, verification compares against the target argmax and never reads cached draft logits, so this can't come from this change.
- **DSV4.1 GSM8K t1, 0.816 → 0.807:** not significant (Welch p≈0.3). This model's t1 accuracy varies a lot from seed to seed (0.78–0.83).

commits.pr_title: [Perf][Kimi K3] Opt-in KV-balanced FP8 MLA decode for agentic workloads
commits.pr_body:
<!-- markdownlint-disable -->

## Overview

Adds an opt-in MLA attention backend for Kimi-K3 on Blackwell, `--attention-backend KIMI_K3_KV_BALANCED_MLA`. Its decode splits each request's KV by its own length, so the decode stays balanced across the GPU when the context lengths in one batch differ a lot, as they do in agentic workloads. It is a standalone backend built on the common MLA backend classes (`MLACommonBackend`, `MLACommonImpl`, `MLACommonMetadataBuilder`); it does not depend on `TOKENSPEED_MLA`. The code lives in `vllm/models/kimi_k3/nvidia/kv_balanced_mla/`. Outside it, the PR only adds the backend's entry to `AttentionBackendEnum` (as the DeepSeek V4, MiniMax M3 and Step5 backends in `vllm/models/` have).

## Claims

- **Decode attention, AgentX context lengths on GB300:** 1.34–1.59x faster than `TOKENSPEED_MLA` with `tokenspeed_mla_min_split_kv=8`, and 1.91–2.67x faster than its default (geometric mean over batch sizes, DEP16 and DCP8, target verify and draft).
- **End-to-end, AgentX on GB300:**
  - DEP16 decode (3P1D c336): +7.8% TPS/GPU and +20% p90 interactivity.
  - DCP8 decode: +4.6% TPS/GPU and +10% p90 interactivity at 3P4D c240, and +2.7% / +13% at the prefill-bound 2P3D c240.
  - The baseline is `TOKENSPEED_MLA` with `tokenspeed_mla_min_split_kv=8`, the setting these recipes already use.
- **Accuracy:** gsm8k with real speculative rejection on the latest revision is 0.961 (DEP16) and 0.967 (DCP8).
- **Opt-in.** The backend is never selected automatically; without `--attention-backend KIMI_K3_KV_BALANCED_MLA` nothing changes.

## Validation

**Unit tests** (`tests/models/kimi_k3/test_kv_balanced_mla.py`, 12 tests, passing on GB300). They check the kernel against an FP32 reference for:
- unequal lengths and an empty request;
- the DSpark draft block (non-causal);
- a DCP8 shard on rank 0, and on rank 5 with interleave 64. The rank-5 lengths end inside that rank's chunks, so the causal mask cuts its last keys. Passing the wrong rank or interleave gives about 80% error, versus 2% when correct.
- a peaked softmax that fails without the P prescale;
- plan plus decode captured in a CUDA graph and replayed with KV lengths changed in place;
- a shared workspace larger than 2 GiB.

The backend tests check that `KIMI_K3_KV_BALANCED_MLA` resolves to this backend, its builder and its base-2 LSE convention, and is in no platform's priority list; that selection rejects an FP16 model, a non-FP8 KV cache, a non-SM10x GPU and a `kv_lora_rank` other than 512; and that `forward_mqa` only runs the kernel. The decode tests check one plan per forward, the DCP path with the LSE, and that a step the kernel can't run raises a `ValueError`.

**Microbenchmark.** Time per decode step on one rank, from CUDA-graph replays, mean of 5 random batches per N. Context lengths are sampled from the AgentX trace (median about 98K tokens, p90 about 284K). Every variant decodes the same requests and was checked against an FP32 reference.
- `ts1` is `TOKENSPEED_MLA` with the default `tokenspeed_mla_min_split_kv=1`.
- `ts8` is the same with `tokenspeed_mla_min_split_kv=8`.
- `kvb` is this PR's decode, excluding its plan. The plan takes 4–13 µs, runs once per forward and is shared by all MLA layers.

| Decode | Step | kvb vs ts1 | kvb vs ts8 |
|---|---|---|---|
| DEP16: 96 heads, full KV | verify (q=5, causal) | 2.63x (1.93–3.30) | 1.37x (1.25–1.54) |
| DEP16 | draft (64 heads, q=4) | 2.67x (1.17–4.39) | 1.34x (1.17–1.47) |
| DCP8: 96 gathered heads, 1/8 KV shard, LSE | verify | 1.91x (1.34–3.33) | 1.52x (1.41–1.70) |
| DCP8 | draft | 2.46x (1.78–3.32) | 1.59x (1.48–1.82) |

<details>
<summary>Per batch size (µs)</summary>

| Decode | Step | N | ts1 | ts8 | kvb | kvb vs ts1 | kvb vs ts8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| DEP16 | verify | 4 | 402.1 | 308.7 | 208.5 | 1.93x | 1.48x |
| DEP16 | verify | 8 | 928.3 | 433.6 | 281.1 | 3.30x | 1.54x |
| DEP16 | verify | 16 | 2335.6 | 1017.3 | 759.1 | 3.08x | 1.34x |
| DEP16 | verify | 24 | 2744.4 | 1341.3 | 1045.3 | 2.63x | 1.28x |
| DEP16 | verify | 32 | 4374.5 | 2223.9 | 1783.0 | 2.45x | 1.25x |
| DEP16 | draft | 4 | 189.5 | 189.5 | 161.4 | 1.17x | 1.17x |
| DEP16 | draft | 8 | 470.6 | 295.2 | 203.7 | 2.31x | 1.45x |
| DEP16 | draft | 16 | 1175.5 | 593.9 | 403.6 | 2.91x | 1.47x |
| DEP16 | draft | 24 | 2473.4 | 764.9 | 563.3 | 4.39x | 1.36x |
| DEP16 | draft | 32 | 3778.6 | 1245.7 | 964.9 | 3.92x | 1.29x |
| DCP8 | verify | 16 | 295.5 | 151.3 | 88.7 | 3.33x | 1.70x |
| DCP8 | verify | 32 | 413.3 | 293.1 | 189.1 | 2.19x | 1.55x |
| DCP8 | verify | 64 | 763.2 | 640.3 | 430.8 | 1.77x | 1.49x |
| DCP8 | verify | 96 | 984.9 | 971.1 | 662.0 | 1.49x | 1.47x |
| DCP8 | verify | 128 | 1189.6 | 1251.3 | 888.6 | 1.34x | 1.41x |
| DCP8 | draft | 16 | 159.5 | 91.9 | 50.5 | 3.16x | 1.82x |
| DCP8 | draft | 32 | 340.5 | 168.1 | 102.7 | 3.32x | 1.64x |
| DCP8 | draft | 64 | 561.5 | 350.5 | 228.6 | 2.46x | 1.53x |
| DCP8 | draft | 96 | 668.0 | 508.4 | 339.1 | 1.97x | 1.50x |
| DCP8 | draft | 128 | 780.4 | 649.2 | 438.4 | 1.78x | 1.48x |

</details>

**End-to-end.**
- **Setup:** Kimi-K3 MXFP4 on GB300 NVL72, using the InferenceX AgentX agentic-coding replay with Dynamo disaggregated serving, Mooncake KV offload, and DSpark speculative decoding with 4 tokens (synthetic acceptance, as the recipes use).
- **Builds:** both sides run the same vLLM main build. The only difference is the decode workers' decode kernel. These runs used this PR's earlier revision, which selected the same kernel and dispatch through `additional_config` instead of the attention backend name. A rerun of the DEP16 point on the latest revision gave the same result.
- **Baseline:** the decode workers use `TOKENSPEED_MLA` with `tokenspeed_mla_min_split_kv=8`.
- **Runs:** one run per side for each point. A repeat of the DEP16 pair gave +8.6% TPS/GPU.

| Config | TPS/GPU | Interactivity p50 / p90 (tok/s) | E2E latency p90 | TTFT mean / p90 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3P1D, TP8 prefill + DEP16 decode, c336: baseline | 27,267 | 38.1 / 35.2 | 60.6 s | 3.14 / 5.82 s |
| same, KV-balanced | **29,402 (+7.8%)** | 45.8 / 42.4 (+20% / +20%) | 53.9 s (−11%) | 4.22 / 9.69 s |
| 3P4D, DCP8 prefill + DCP8 decode, c240: baseline | 20,421 | 75.7 / 68.9 | 33.3 s | 1.89 / 3.03 s |
| same, KV-balanced | **21,370 (+4.6%)** | 83.1 / 75.9 (+10% / +10%) | 30.8 s (−7%) | 1.84 / 2.94 s |
| 2P3D, DCP8 prefill + DCP8 decode, c240: baseline | 24,503 | 63.7 / 58.0 | 43.9 s | 5.21 / 10.74 s |
| same, KV-balanced | **25,162 (+2.7%)** | 72.6 / 65.3 (+14% / +13%) | 40.7 s (−7%) | 5.83 / 12.41 s |

- **Why TTFT rises at 3P1D and 2P3D:** a faster decode lets more requests through, which puts more load on the prefill workers that limit those points. At 3P4D, with more prefill capacity, TTFT improves slightly.
- **Why DCP8 gains less:** with DCP8, MLA attention is a smaller share of each decode step than with DEP16.

**Accuracy.** gsm8k (5-shot, lm-eval) with real speculative rejection, `KIMI_K3_KV_BALANCED_MLA` on the decode workers (latest revision). Every decode step ran on the kernel.

| Config | strict-match | flexible-extract | Acceptance length |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1P1D, TP8 prefill + DEP16 decode | 0.961 | 0.961 | 3.61 |
| 1P1D, DCP8 prefill + DCP8 decode | 0.967 | 0.967 | 3.27 |

**CI.** The B200 Kimi K3 step (`models/kimi_k3`) runs the new tests. They were validated on GB300 (SM103) and not run on B200 (SM100). On the MI355 step the tests are skipped, and the test module imports without the CuTe kernel.

## Details

**KV imbalance in agentic decode.** An agentic decode batch mixes very different context lengths, for example 5K, 20K, 98K and 300K tokens. To spread one request's attention over the GPU, the decode cuts its KV into splits; clusters process the splits in parallel and a reduction merges them. `TOKENSPEED_MLA`, the existing FP8 MLA decode for this model, uses one split count for the whole batch: it's chosen from the batch size and SM count, with `tokenspeed_mla_min_split_kv` as a floor. With a skewed batch, any single count is wrong for most requests:
- **Too many splits for short requests.** Short requests are cut into tiny splits that each pay the per-split setup and the reduction.
- **Too few splits for long requests.** The longest requests leave a tail in which a few clusters stream hundreds of thousands of keys while the rest of the GPU is idle.

`min_split_kv=8` helps the long requests and hurts the short ones; at DCP8 N=128 it is slower than the default (see `ts8` vs `ts1`).

**What the KV-balanced decode does:**
1. **Plan.** A Triton planner gives each request its own split count from its KV length: 1 to 8 splits of at least 1024 tokens, sized to fill at most 8 waves of the GPU's clusters. It writes the planned (query tile, request, split) entries as a device work list. It reads nothing on the host, so it is captured in the decode CUDA graph. It runs once per forward, and every MLA layer reuses it.
2. **Execute.** One wave of persistent 2-CTA clusters walks the work list, so every cluster gets about the same amount of KV.
3. **Skip the merge where possible.** A request planned as a single split stores its final output directly, and the reduction skips it.
4. **Keep small probabilities.** Long splits can make probabilities small enough to flush to zero in E4M3, so P is stored scaled by 2^6 and the LSE removes the factor.

**Code layout** (`vllm/models/kimi_k3/nvidia/kv_balanced_mla/`):
- `kernel.py` and `helpers.py`: TokenSpeed MLA 2.0.3's FP8 decode kernel (MIT), vendored with the changes above. Compared with the release, the kernel adds 347 lines (including renames and casts so it passes `typos` and mypy) and drops its 1,252-line benchmark harness; the helpers add 59 lines, the work-list tile scheduler. They do not import the `tokenspeed_mla` package at runtime.
- `core.py`: the planner and the compiled kernel.
- `decode.py`: the per-layer dispatch: the once-per-forward plan, the DCP arguments and the shape checks.
- `backend.py`: `KimiK3KvBalancedMLABackend`, `KimiK3KvBalancedMLAMetadataBuilder` and `KimiK3KvBalancedMLAImpl`. The impl's `forward_mqa` runs the kernel.
- `vllm/v1/attention/backends/registry.py`: the `KIMI_K3_KV_BALANCED_MLA` entry.

Kimi-K3's MLA layer (`mla.py`) is unchanged: it calls the selected backend's `forward_mqa`.

**Why a standalone backend.** The backend is about 190 lines on the common MLA classes, and it states everything the kernel relies on itself, so a later change to `TOKENSPEED_MLA` can't silently change what this backend runs:
- the FP8 KV cache layout (576 values per token, pages of 32 or 64);
- the decode metadata (`seq_lens`, `block_table`, `dcp_tot_seq_lens`) with uniform query lengths and `UNIFORM_BATCH` CUDA graphs;
- the packed FP8 query from the common MLA impl;
- the base-2 LSE convention of the DCP combine (`lse_base_on_e=False`);
- non-causal multi-token decode for the DSpark draft, with and without DCP.

Prefill uses the configured MLA prefill backend, as in the other MLA backends.

**Supported configurations.** An FP8 E4M3 KV cache, an SM10x GPU, a BF16 model and MLA dimensions (`qk_nope_head_dim`, `qk_rope_head_dim`, `v_head_dim`, `kv_lora_rank`) = (128, 64, 128, 512); backend selection rejects anything else with the reason. Alibi, sliding window, soft cap and non-decoder attention raise a `ValueError` when the layer is built. The kernel also needs more than 64 query rows per request (heads × query tokens) and at most as many requests as it plans for; the head count isn't known at selection, so these fail at model build with a `ValueError`. There is no fallback decode: a decode step the kernel can't run raises a `ValueError` with the reason. In the end-to-end runs every decode shape (target verify q=1–5, draft q=4) ran on the kernel. `cp_kv_cache_interleave_size` is read from the parallel config on every call, since NIXL P/D sets it after the model is built. The DSpark draft takes its backend from the speculative config's `attention_backend`.

**Tradeoffs and limitations:**
- **Size:** the vendored kernel adds about 4.9K lines. Integrating through the `tokenspeed_mla` package instead (reusing its compiled kernel with planned per-request splits) gave about 20% less speedup in our microbenchmarks. The work-list scheduler, direct output and P prescale need kernel changes.
- **Memory:** the split-KV scratch is sized as requests × query tiles × 8 splits of FP16 partial outputs. That's about 0.5 GB for 128 requests at heads=96, q=5, versus about 0.23 GB for TokenSpeed's SM-based bound; it's logged at startup.
- **Host syncs:** by inspection, the decode path adds none. Planning is a device kernel, and the once-per-forward check compares the forward context and a data pointer. This was not checked with `VLLM_GPU_SYNC_CHECK=error`.

commits.pr_title: [CI] List one test path per line in Buildkite pytest commands to avoid merge conflicts
commits.pr_body:
## Overview

Many Buildkite commands list several test files (or `--ignore` / `--deselect` paths) on one line, e.g. `models_basic.yaml` runs 13 files in a single 500-character `pytest` line. Two PRs that each add a test to the same job conflict on that line. This PR puts every test path on its own line, with no change to what CI runs.

## Claims

- Every pytest command that names 2 or more paths (counting `--ignore` / `--deselect`) now has one path per line: ~105 commands in `test_areas/`, `test-amd.yaml`, `intel_jobs/`, `hardware_tests/cpu.yaml`, `run-intel-ci-test.sh`, plus the L4 2-node command in `distributed.yaml`.
- No CI behavior change: all edited yaml loads to the same command strings as `main`.
- `check_test_tethering.py` now joins `\`-continued lines. Without this, the `|`-block edits here would make the tethering gate count every test as tethered.
- `tests/AGENTS.md` documents the convention.

## Validation

- **Same commands.** `yaml.safe_load` of each of the 25 edited `>-` yaml files equals `main`. The 2 `|`-block files (`cpu.yaml`, `models_distributed.yaml`) and `run-intel-ci-test.sh` equal `main` once `\`+newline is joined (what bash does). `bash -n` passes.
- **Same pipelines.** The ci-infra pipeline generator (`vllm-project/ci-infra` e28b4ff355) produces byte-identical step scripts for every `>-` file. `test-amd.yaml` rendered through `test-template-amd.j2` with `minijinja-cli` is byte-identical to `main` across 8 `mirror_hw` values x 3 modes. Intel yaml strings were also compared with PyYAML, libyaml, and go-yaml v3 (`yq`).
- **Same tethering.** `python tools/pre_commit/check_test_tethering.py --all` prints the same output as on `main` (exit 0), and the normalized `load_selections()` list is identical.
- **Checker tests.** `pytest tests/tools/test_check_test_tethering.py`: 143 passed. 3 of the 5 new cases fail with `main`'s checker; the other 2 are a positive control and a guard for an escaped `\\` before a newline.
- `pre-commit run --files <changed files>` passes.
- No `.buildkite` command still names 2 or more test paths on one line, except the line noted under Details.

<details>
<summary>Reproduce the "same commands" check</summary>

```python
import re, subprocess, yaml

def norm(v):  # join shell `\` continuations, as bash does
    if isinstance(v, str):
        return re.sub(r" \\\n *", " ", v)
    if isinstance(v, list):
        return [norm(x) for x in v]
    if isinstance(v, dict):
        return {k: norm(x) for k, x in v.items()}
    return v

base = subprocess.check_output(["git", "merge-base", "origin/main", "HEAD"], text=True).strip()
files = subprocess.check_output(
    ["git", "diff", "--name-only", base, "HEAD", "--", ".buildkite/"], text=True
).split()
for f in files:
    old = subprocess.check_output(["git", "show", f"{base}:{f}"], text=True)
    new = open(f).read()
    if f.endswith(".sh"):
        same = norm(new) == old
    else:
        same = norm(yaml.safe_load(new)) == norm(yaml.safe_load(old))
    print("OK  " if same else "DIFF", f)
```

</details>

## Details

**Format.** Single-line commands become `>-` folded blocks: `pytest -v -s` on the first line, then one path per line. Option groups (`-k '...'`, `-m x`, `--shard-id=.. --num-shards=..`) stay on one line, and argument order is unchanged. `>-` is already used in `engine.yaml`, `compile.yaml`, and the Intel jobs, and every line in it is literal text, so `#` or `: ` in a `-k` expression cannot break the yaml. Lines inside existing `>-` blocks are split in place. Lines inside `|` blocks use shell `\` continuations, as `cpu.yaml` already does.

Two rules when editing a `>-` block:
- Keep every line at the same indent. A more-indented line keeps its newline.
- Delete a path line instead of commenting it out. A `#` line turns the rest of the command into a shell comment.

**Tethering checker.** `_split_shell_stages` tokenizes with `shlex`, which keeps an escaped newline inside the token. Existing `cpu.yaml` blocks only worked because `normalize_test_path` strips the leading `\n`. An indented continuation, as in `models_distributed.yaml` here, yields a bare `"\n"` token. It normalizes to `""`, which matches every test, so the full scan reported all 26 allowlist entries as "now tethered". A continued `--ignore` (`"\n--ignore=..."`) was also read as a path. The fix joins odd runs of backslash + newline before tokenizing, the same as `_parse_shell_script` already does for scripts. It changes no selection parsed from `main`'s pipelines.

**Scope.**
- The rule is 2 or more paths, so it is easy to state and check. 39 of the rewritten commands are a directory plus one `--ignore`.
- The few existing hanging-indent lists in `kernels.yaml` / `test-amd.yaml` are already one path per line and are left as they are.
- Not changed: `intel_jobs/models_multimodal_intel.yaml:76` is missing a trailing `&&` (since #59865), so `pytest ... -m core_model pytest -v -s .../test_qwen2_vl.py` runs as a single call. That changes behavior, so it is fixed separately in #TBD.

commits.pr_body: ## Purpose `:amd: (MI300) Language Models (Extended Generation)` lost its pod (exit -7, "Perhaps the container was OOM-killed?") in 3 of its last 5 runs: [amd-ci#15340](https://buildkite.com/vllm/amd-ci/builds/15340), [amd-ci#15350](https://buildkite.com/vllm/amd-ci/builds/15350) and [amd-ci#15384](https://buildkite.com/vllm/amd-ci/builds/15384). The tests in `tests/models/language/generation` load many checkpoints in one pytest process, and their page cache is charged to the pod's memory cgroup. The job reads ~208 GiB of checkpoints against ~133 GiB of effective pod memory, so even passing runs drop below 1 GiB of available RAM. This PR adds an autouse fixture in this directory that frees the previous test's checkpoint page cache when the model changes, using the same mechanism #61415 added for LM Eval. commits.pr_title: [Perf][MoE] Size the DeepGEMM MegaMoE symmetric buffer for one sequence-parallel shard
commits.pr_body:
## Overview With `--moe-backend deep_gemm_mega_moe`, `--enable-expert-parallel`, TP > 1 and PP = 1, Kimi K3 runs its MoE layers sequence parallel: each rank feeds MegaMoE at most `cdiv(max_num_batched_tokens, tp_size)` tokens. The MegaMoE symmetric buffer is still sized for `max_num_batched_tokens` tokens per rank. This PR sizes it for the shard. ## Claims - Kimi K3, `-tp 8 --enable-expert-parallel`, `--max-num-batched-tokens 16384`: MegaMoE buffer per GPU **10.73 GiB → 2.50 GiB**. - MegaMoE outputs do not depend on the buffer size (bitwise equal in a one-off check). ## Validation **Buffer per GPU** (one buffer shared by all MoE layers), allocated on GB300 by the vendored DeepGEMM with the arguments `KimiMoE` passes: 896 experts, top-k 16, `routed_expert_hidden_size` 3584, intermediate 3072, `fp8xfp4`, `situ`, no fused shared experts. EP = TP, DP = 1; TP8 ran on two 4-GPU nodes. | TP = EP | `--max-num-batched-tokens` | main | this PR | |---|---|---|---| | 8 | 16384 | 10.73 GiB | 2.50 GiB | | 8 | 32768 | 21.29 GiB | 3.68 GiB | | 4 | 8192 | 3.74 GiB | 1.66 GiB | | 4 | 16384 | 6.52 GiB | 2.34 GiB | | 4 | 32768 | 12.80 GiB | 3.74 GiB | DeepGEMM rounds the per-rank token bound up to a multiple of 1920 before sizing (the TP8 shard of 2048 tokens is sized for 3840).
Repro ```python # torchrun --nproc-per-node 4 buf.py (TP8: 2 nodes x 4) import os, sys, torch, torch.distributed as dist from vllm.utils.deep_gemm import _import_deep_gemm dist.init_process_group("nccl") torch.cuda.set_device(int(os.environ["LOCAL_RANK"])) buf = _import_deep_gemm().get_symm_buffer_for_mega_moe( dist.group.WORLD, 896, int(sys.argv[1]), 16, 3584, 3072, mma_type="fp8xfp4", activation="situ") if dist.get_rank() == 0: print(f"{buf.buffer.nbytes / 2**30:.2f} GiB") ```
**Checks** on GB300, nightly image for main `c50aca144` + this diff: - Bitwise check (one-off, not added to CI per review): on one GPU with a small MXFP4 layer, buffers with 1920- and 15360-token capacity give `torch.equal` outputs at 1, 7, 48, 500 and 1920 tokens; 1921 tokens is rejected. - `pytest tests/kernels/moe/test_deep_gemm_mega_moe.py tests/models/kimi_k3/test_sequence_parallel.py`: 132 passed. - `pre-commit`: pass. ## Details - **Why it is safe:** DeepGEMM sizes every region from `num_max_tokens_per_rank`. Its expert ring assumes every EP rank sends its full `num_max_tokens_per_rank`, so routing imbalance fits. With sequence parallelism each rank's MoE input is its shard, at most `cdiv(max_num_batched_tokens, tp_size)` rows at any DP size. The DeepGEMM warmup already uses this bound, and `forward()` raises above it. - **Why outputs match:** DeepGEMM picks `BLOCK_M` from the token count, not from the buffer capacity. - **Scope:** `DeepGemmMegaMoEExperts` gets an optional `max_num_tokens` (default unchanged); only `KimiMoE` passes the shard bound. DeepSeek-V4 has the same sequence-parallel MegaMoE path and is left for a follow-up. - **Not validated end-to-end yet:** no `vllm serve` run of Kimi K3 with this change, and no KV-cache measurement. - **Not a duplicate:** no open PR changes the token bound of this buffer. Draft #53556 adds fused shared-expert space to the same buffer. #54347 enables Kimi K3 sequence parallelism with PP, where this bound also holds. - **AI assistance:** Claude Code drafted the code and description, and ran the measurements and checks above at my direction. ---
